commands.name: dataviz
commands.description: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

commands.name: update-config
commands.description: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

content.text:
**The Keeper's Jar**

For thirty-one years, Ada Pelham kept the light at Scarrow Head. For most of those years she also kept a mason jar of sea glass on the sill of the watch room, between the brass barometer and the logbook with its swollen cover.

It started as a joke. The summer they arrived, her husband, Walt, came back from the rocks at low tide with his pockets clinking. "Every keeper needs a hobby that doesn't involve the sea," he said, emptying a fistful of green and brown shards onto the kitchen table. "Or one that involves it in a smaller way."

Ada laughed, then picked up a piece of cobalt the size of a fingernail and held it to the window. The light came through it blue. She had been holding up sea glass to the light ever since.

The rules were simple. You took only what the tide had finished with: edges worn soft, surfaces frosted and milky, glass rounded by years of rolling against stone. A bottle with a sharp lip was just trash waiting to finish its work. "The sea takes its time," Walt used to say. "You don't rush the job, and you don't steal it early."

Over three decades the jar filled. They bought a second jar, then a cake tin, then a cardboard box for the overflow. Ada sorted on Sunday afternoons: white, which was most common, then brown from old ale bottles, then green from wine and soda. The rare pieces she kept apart. There was aqua, lavender from old manganese glass, and once a single red that had made Walt whistle.

Walt died in the winter of the eleventh year. A stroke took him in the kitchen. When she found the cake tin afterward, she didn't cry. She sat on the floor with it in her lap and sorted the shards by feel with her eyes closed. She kept doing that, walking the tideline after storms, bending for every frosted edge, until her pockets were full.

In September, the Northern Lights Authority wrote to say that Scarrow Head would be automated by the end of the month. Sensors and a satellite-timed lamp would do her work, and the station would be locked and left to the gulls. She read the letter three times at the kitchen table, feeling mostly relief, and then a grief she couldn't explain to the young inspector who came to take inventory.

"Anything you'd like to take with you, Mrs. Pelham?" he asked, glancing at the jars.

"Only what's mine," she said.

On her last night she didn't sleep. At midnight she climbed the iron stairs one final time, checked the lamp, wound the clockwork that turned the lens, and wrote in the logbook: *Light burning. Wind northwest, moderate. Visibility good. Sea calm.* She paused, then added: *Relieved by machine. Keeper signing off.*

Then she went down the path to the cove.

The tide was out, leaving the rocks slick and silver under the lamp's sweep, which passed over her every nineteen seconds. She walked the wrack line with a torch, though she hardly needed it. She knew this beach the way she knew the stairs. Her hands searched while her mind wandered.

Near a split boulder, where shingle gave way to coarse sand, something caught the torchlight. She knelt. It was small and so worn it had lost every corner, its surface clouded like breath on a cold window. She rubbed it with her thumb, and beneath the grime a true blue showed through.

She had found cobalt before. She had never found this shade, deep as the sea just before dawn. It occurred to her that she had been looking for it for thirty years without knowing it had a color.

She sat on the cold stone and held the glass up toward the lamp. For a moment the beam crossed it and it glowed. Then the light swept on into the dark, and the stone was only stone again.

Ada thought about how long the sea had taken to make this. Years of sand and salt and rolling, a bottle thrown from a ship or a kitchen window, broken and abandoned, worn down until nothing sharp was left. Nobody had planned it. Nobody needed it. It was simply what the water did to things it had patience for.

She thought, too, about the light above her, which would keep turning without anyone to wind it. She thought about the keepers before her, and the ships that had passed safely in the dark because someone had climbed those stairs every night.

She put the blue glass in her coat pocket, beside the handkerchief Walt had given her the year they arrived. Then she walked back up the path, counting the steps out of habit, and didn't look back until she reached the gate.

At the top, the lamp swept over her once, then twice. Then it turned away toward the open sea, steady and bright, and she let it go.
